Fish Gate
FISH gate
proper noun
From the Hebrew sha’ar hadagím, “gate of the fishes,” so called from the fish brought in by it to the markets of the city.

📖 Biblical Definition

The fish gate was builded in Nehemiah’s day by the sons of Hassenaah, who “laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof” (Neh 3:3). By it the men of Tyre and the fishers brought their fish into the city, and a market stood near at hand. It was an ancient gate, for Manasseh king of Judah, after his humbling, “built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entering in at the fish gate” (2Chr 33:14). The prophet Zephaniah heard the judgment of the LORD draw near by it: “the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills” (Zep 1:10). At the dedication the companies passed “above the fish gate” (Neh 12:39). So the gate where men brought up their nets and their catch became a watchword both of common trade and of coming judgment; and the people of God, who pass daily in and out at such gates, are bidden to do their business in the fear of the LORD, and to remember that the same city which buys and sells shall give account to Him who judgeth righteously.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A gate of Jerusalem, built by the sons of Hassenaah, named from the fish brought in by it.

expand to see more

FISH GATE, a gate of the wall of Jerusalem, named from the fish brought in by it to the markets.

The name signifies the gate of the fishes, after the Hebrew tongue.

It was built by the sons of Hassenaah in the rebuilding under Nehemiah.

It was an ancient gate, mentioned also in the days of Manasseh and Zephaniah.

It witnesses both to the common labour of men and to the judgment of the LORD.

📖 Key Scripture

Neh 3:3 — "But the fish gate did the sons of Hassenaah build, who also laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, the locks thereof, and the bars thereof."

2Chr 33:14 — "Now after this he built a wall without the city of David, on the west side of Gihon, in the valley, even to the entering in at the fish gate, and compassed about Ophel, and raised it up a very great height, and put captains of war in all the fenced cities of Judah."

Zep 1:10 — "And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD, that there shall be the noise of a cry from the fish gate, and an howling from the second, and a great crashing from the hills."

Neh 12:39 — "And from above the gate of Ephraim, and above the old gate, and above the fish gate, and the tower of Hananeel, and the tower of Meah, even unto the sheep gate: and they stood still in the prison gate."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A gate of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses to the labour of men and the judgment of the LORD upon the city.

expand to see more

The fish gate is a plain gate of an ancient wall, where the fishers brought their catch to market, and no movement of the present age has set itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader may know it for a true gate of a true city.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the common business of life is done before the face of God: the same gate that received the daily trade of the city was named by the prophet as a place of coming judgment. Let the people of God buy and sell and labour in the fear of the LORD, who weigheth the city in His balances.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for “gate of the fishes,” named for the fish brought in by it.

expand to see more

Fish Gate — Hebrew sha’ar hadagím, “gate of the fishes.”

It was named for the fish brought in by it to the markets.

The sons of Hassenaah built it in the rebuilding under Nehemiah.

It was an ancient gate, known in the days of Manasseh.

Zephaniah named it as a place of coming judgment upon the city.

Usage

"By the fish gate the city did its business; let the saints do their business unto the LORD."

"The gate of common trade was also the gate of warning: judgment waits upon the careless city."

"He who calls fishers to follow Him still gathers men as a net gathereth of every kind."
